title: Pollution haven hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that polluting firms move production to countries with weaker environmental rules, because strict rules make production more expensive.

facts.text: It has three strengths: pollution costs matter at the margin; they measurably shift trade and investment; or countries deliberately set standards too low to attract investment.
The first two versions have empirical support, but how much the effect matters next to other trade and investment factors is disputed.
Economists model economic activity as falling with regulatory stringency, because regulation raises input costs and erodes comparative advantage in pollution-intensive goods.
Stringency is hard to measure, since compliance costs take many forms: taxes, delays, lawsuits, product redesign or emission limits.
After the US tightened lead air standards in 2009, exports of used lead-acid batteries to Mexico rose four-fold, followed by more low-birth-weight babies near Mexican recycling plants.
It may help explain the environmental Kuznets curve: rich countries' cleaner environments may partly come from shifting dirty production to poorer ones.
Standard theory says standards should differ between places with different abatement costs and assimilative capacity, so some relocation need not be inefficient.

contested_note: Economists dispute how strong the effect is; Paul Krugman doubted major real-world examples exist, while some studies find significant effects.
